detailedInstruction:
Welcome to Python programming! Python is beginner-friendly and powerful:

1. Open Visual Studio Code (VSCode)
2. Navigate to your workspace folder
3. Right-click in the file explorer
4. Select 'New File' from the context menu
5. Name the file 'hello.py' (note the .py extension)
6. Press Enter to create the file

Why .py extension: This tells your computer and editor that this file contains Python code. Python files don't need compilation like Java - they run directly!
hint: Right-click in workspace, select 'New File', name it 'hello.py'
errorCorrection: Make sure the extension is .py, not .txt

detailedInstruction:
Python is known for its simplicity. Your first program is just one line:

```python
print("Hello, World!")
```

That's it! Unlike Java, Python doesn't need:
• Class definitions for simple programs
• A main method
• Semicolons at the end of lines
• Curly braces for simple statements

Type this line in your hello.py file. Notice how clean and readable Python is!
errorCorrection: Make sure you have parentheses around the text in quotes

detailedInstruction:
Running Python is simple - no compilation needed:

1. Save your hello.py file (Ctrl+S or Cmd+S)
2. Open the terminal in VSCode (View → Terminal)
3. Type this command and press Enter:
   python hello.py
   
   OR (if python doesn't work):
   python3 hello.py

What happens:
• Python interpreter reads your .py file directly
• It executes each line of code immediately
• No intermediate compilation step needed
• You should see 'Hello, World!' printed

This is called 'interpreted' vs 'compiled' language!
hint: In terminal, type 'python hello.py' or 'python3 hello.py'

detailedInstruction:
Python variables are very flexible - no type declarations needed:

```python
# Create variables.py
# Comments start with # in Python

# Variables - Python figures out the type automatically
name = "Alex"          # String (text)
age = 25               # Integer (whole number)
height = 5.9           # Float (decimal number)
is_student = True      # Boolean (True/False)

# Print variables
print("Name:", name)
print("Age:", age)
print("Height:", height, "feet")
print("Student:", is_student)

# Python can change variable types!
age = "twenty-five"    # Now age is a string!
print("Age as text:", age)
```

Create variables.py and try this!
hint: Create variables.py file and copy the code
errorCorrection: Python is case-sensitive: True, False with capital letters

detailedInstruction:
Getting user input in Python is simple with input():

```python
# Create user_input.py

# Get user input (always returns a string)
name = input("What's your name? ")
print("Hello", name + "!")

# For numbers, convert the input
age_text = input("How old are you? ")
age = int(age_text)  # Convert string to integer

print(f"You are {age} years old.")  # f-string formatting
print(f"Next year you'll be {age + 1}!")

# One-liner for numbers
height = float(input("Your height in feet: "))
print(f"You are {height} feet tall.")
```

Create user_input.py and make it interactive!
hint: Use input() for text, int() to convert to numbers
errorCorrection: Remember to convert input() to int() or float() for numbers

detailedInstruction:
Python uses indentation instead of braces for code blocks:

```python
# Create conditions.py

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))

# Note: Python uses indentation (4 spaces) instead of {}
if age >= 18:
    print("You are an adult!")
    print("You can vote!")
elif age >= 13:  # 'elif' instead of 'else if'
    print("You are a teenager!")
    print("Enjoy your youth!")
else:
    print("You are a child!")
    print("Keep learning and growing!")

# Multiple conditions
if age >= 16 and age < 18:
    print("You can drive but can't vote yet.")

if age == 21:
    print("Special birthday!")
```

Create conditions.py and test different ages!
hint: Remember: indentation matters in Python! Use 4 spaces.
errorCorrection: Check indentation - all code in if/else blocks must be indented

detailedInstruction:
Python loops are clean and readable:

```python
# Create loops.py

# For loop with range()
print("Counting to 5:")
for i in range(1, 6):  # range(start, stop) - stop is excluded
    print(f"Count: {i}")

# For loop with lists
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "orange"]
print("\nMy fruits:")
for fruit in fruits:
    print(f"I like {fruit}")

# While loop
print("\nCountdown:")
countdown = 5
while countdown > 0:
    print(countdown)
    countdown -= 1  # Same as countdown = countdown - 1
print("Blast off!")

# List comprehension (advanced but cool!)
squares = [x**2 for x in range(1, 6)]
print(f"\nSquares: {squares}")
```

Create loops.py and explore Python's loop power!
